outcome: Nothing has happened to the BI-group question since 26 January 2024 that I could find: the classification of BI-groups is still open, the only BI-specific results I found date from 2015 and 2017 (the 2015 paper unverified, the 2017 preprint read from its abstract), and the events inside the window concern namesake problems or neighbouring isomorphism properties (CI, DCI), not BI-groups.
problem_asks: (1) Which finite groups G are BI-groups? Wikipedia's definition: G is a BI-group if, for all inverse-closed subsets S and T of G minus {1}, Cay(G,S) isomorphic to Cay(G,T) implies M_nu^S = M_nu^T for every positive integer nu, where M_nu^S is the set of sums of chi(s) over s in S, taken over the irreducible characters chi of G with chi(1) = nu. This asks for the full list of such groups, i.e. a classification. (2) Within (1), the yes/no sub-question Babai's background asks, as the 2017 preprint's abstract reports it: is every finite group a BI-group? Answering (1) answers (2). (3) Not in the Wikipedia wording: Babai's own 1979 formulation, as secondary sources report it, asks the same invariance for all Cayley digraphs, not only inverse-closed (undirected) connection sets. Recorded as context only; it is not part of the statement given.

events.what_happened: Alireza Abdollahi and Maysam Zallaghi posted arXiv:1710.04446 (one version, v1 of 12 Oct 2017), 'Non-abelian finite groups whose character sums are invariant but are not Cayley isomorphism'. Per its abstract (read from the arXiv abstract page through a fetch that paraphrased it, with the key sentence quoted): the authors find two non-abelian BI-groups, of orders 20 and 42, which are not CI-groups, and they list all BI-groups of order up to 30. The same abstract (also via that fetch) records that every finite CI-group is a BI-group and that all abelian groups are BI-groups. The paper is listed as J. Algebra Appl. 18(1) (2019), article 1950013, DOI 10.1142/S0219498819500130; that journal locator comes from Wikipedia's reference list, and the journal page itself returned HTTP 403, so its acceptance and online dates are unverified. The arXiv PDF returns compressed binary to my tools, so the proofs, the method used for the order-30 list, and the exact list are unverified.
events.revisions: arXiv: v1 only, per the arXiv abstract page. Journal version: JAA 2019 per Wikipedia's reference list. Dates conflict: Wikipedia gives 10 Feb 2019, OpenAlex gives publication date 2018-02-27; not resolved. The v1 PDF outline shows unresolved 'Theorem ??' cross-references, so the journal version may differ from v1.
events.delivers: Exhibits two non-abelian BI-groups, of orders 20 and 42, that are not CI-groups, so for non-abelian groups BI does not coincide with CI. Gives a list of all BI-groups of order at most 30. Restrictions: the list covers orders up to 30 only, and the setting is the inverse-closed (undirected) connection sets of the Wikipedia definition. The abstract does not name any group as non-BI; the non-BI examples the preprint refers to are attributed to the 2015 paper (event abdollahi-zallaghi-2015-character-sums).
events.remains: Parts (1) and (2) of problem_asks remain open. For orders above 30, nothing beyond the two order-20 and order-42 groups is established by this event. Nothing here settles whether every finite group is a BI-group. Babai's digraph version (part 3) is not addressed as far as the abstract shows.

Not a counterexample to anything in the problem. Whether the BI check is explicit or by finite computation is not established from what I could read.

events.what_happened: Yuxuan Li, Binzhou Xia, Sanming Zhou and Wenying Zhu, 'A solution to Babai's problem on digraphs with non-diagonalizable adjacency matrix', arXiv:2208.00887 (v1 1 Aug 2022; v2 12 Sep 2023). The arXiv abstract page (opened) says it answers Babai's problem from Babai's own 1985 work on arc-transitive digraphs with non-diagonalizable adjacency matrices: it constructs an infinite family of s-arc-transitive digraphs for each s >= 2 and an infinite family of vertex-primitive digraphs, all with non-diagonalizable adjacency matrices. Namesake only: this is about diagonalizability, not character sums on Cayley graphs. Published in Combinatorica (2023), per a search result; the Springer page redirected to a login and was not opened.

events.what_happened: Ignacio Garcia-Marco and Kolja Knauer, 'Coloring minimal Cayley graphs', arXiv:2405.19543 (v1 29 May 2024; v2 27 Nov 2024; v3 6 Dec 2024). Per its abstract (opened): Babai raised in 1978 whether minimal Cayley graphs have bounded chromatic number; the authors show minimal Cayley graphs of some generalized dihedral or nilpotent groups have chromatic number at most 3, that soluble groups sometimes need 4 colours, and they construct graphs of unbounded chromatic number with a specific proper edge-colouring, described as a step toward Babai's 1994 conjecture. Namesake only: a chromatic-number question about minimal Cayley graphs, not the character-sum question.

events.what_happened: James Davies, Meike Hatzel and Liana Yepremyan, 'Counterexample to Babai's lonely colour conjecture', arXiv:2410.05199 (one version, v1, 7 Oct 2024). Per the arXiv abstract page (opened): it disproves Babai's 1978 conjecture that no-lonely-colour graphs have bounded chromatic number, by constructing graphs of arbitrarily large girth and chromatic number with a proper edge-colouring in which no cycle contains a colour used exactly once. Motivated by colourings of minimal Cayley graphs. Namesake only: a chromatic-number conjecture, not the character-sum question.
events.delivers: Disproves the lonely colour conjecture (bounded chromatic number of no-lonely-colour graphs). A different question from the BI-group statement; nothing on character sums or BI-groups.

events.what_happened: Grigory Ryabov, 'On CI-property of normal Cayley digraphs over abelian groups', arXiv:2503.00859 (v1, 2 Mar 2025). Per the arXiv abstract page (opened): it reduces the abelian case to abelian p-groups and shows every normal Cayley digraph over an abelian p-group of order at most p^5, for odd p, is CI. The abstract page does not mention BI-groups or character sums. A search summary says it was later published in J. Algebra Appl. (2025, DOI 10.1142/s0219498827500708); not verified. Neighbouring property, not the BI question.
events.delivers: CI-property result for normal Cayley digraphs over abelian p-groups of order at most p^5 (odd p). A different property (CI, not BI). Nothing on BI-groups.

events.what_happened: Ted Dobson, Joy Morris and Pablo Spiga, 'Groups with elements of order 8 do not have the DCI property', arXiv:2404.13938 (one version, v1, 22 Apr 2024). Per the arXiv abstract page (opened, paraphrased by the fetch): C_k semidirect C_8 for odd k, and (C_n x C_3) semidirect C_8 for n an odd multiple of 3, lack the DCI (directed Cayley isomorphism) property, and the paper concludes that no group with an element of order 8 has the DCI property. The abstract page does not mention BI-groups or character sums. Neighbouring property, not the BI question.
events.delivers: Negative DCI results for groups with an element of order 8. A different property (DCI). Nothing on BI-groups.
events.direction: Negative DCI result. Says nothing about BI-groups.

disputes.summary: Several different results are called 'Babai's problem' or carry Babai's name: the BI-group character-sum question (this bullet); Babai's problem on non-diagonalizable adjacency matrices of digraphs (Li, Xia, Zhou, Zhu 2022); Babai's lonely colour conjecture (Davies, Hatzel, Yepremyan 2024); and Babai's minimal Cayley graph problem (García-Marco and Knauer 2024; Davies, Hatzel, Yepremyan 2026). These are not disputes about this problem's status; they are recorded as separate events because a name match alone could lead a reader to count them here.

summary: I ran 34 web searches and opened the sources listed below. The question is Babai's 1979 question, from 'Spectra of Cayley graphs' (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 27(2), 1979), whether the character-sum set M_nu^S is an invariant of Cay(G,S); a group for which it is is a BI-group. The Wikipedia article (fetched through a summarising tool, so not verbatim) lists 'Which finite groups are BI-groups?' as open, gives no classification, and cites three works: Babai 1979, Abdollahi and Zallaghi 2015 (Comm. Algebra, character sums for Cayley graphs), and Abdollahi and Zallaghi 2019 (J. Algebra Appl., the journal version of arXiv:1710.04446). The only BI-specific results I found are these two. The 2017 preprint's abstract (opened) gives two non-abelian BI-groups of orders 20 and 42 that are not CI-groups, and a list of all BI-groups of order at most 30; I could not read its body, so the proofs and the list are unverified. The 2015 paper I could not open (publisher returned 403). The preprint's introduction, as a search excerpt quoted it, describes that paper as presenting examples of finite non-BI-groups, and one search summary says these include S_n for n >= 4. I have not verified either claim, so the record does not treat any group as known non-BI. A close call: if the 2015 examples are as reported, some groups are already known non-BI and the problem is partly settled before the window. That would be a pre-window fact, not a window event, and the Wikipedia wording still marks the question open. Inside the window (since 26 Jan 2024) I found no result about BI-groups. The windowed items I found are namesakes or neighbouring properties: Davies, Hatzel and Yepremyan on the lonely colour conjecture (Oct 2024); García-Marco and Knauer on minimal Cayley graph chromatic number (May 2024); Davies, Hatzel and Yepremyan on minimal Cayley graph chromatic number (Aug 2026, AI-credited to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, the only AI credit among the events); Ryabov on the CI property (Mar 2025); and Dobson, Morris and Spiga on the DCI property (Apr 2024). The 2022 Li, Xia, Zhou and Zhu paper is a namesake about diagonalizability and predates the window. Citation signals are weak: OpenAlex lists zero citations for the 2017 preprint and the 2019 journal article (coverage is partial), and I found no later paper that cites them for BI-groups; Wikipedia's reference list is the only later citer I could confirm. Babai's 1979 paper has 218 citations in OpenAlex, but I did not check which of those discuss Problem 3.3, so it is not recorded as an event: it poses the question and resolves nothing. AI involvement: I searched explicitly for AI and BI-groups or Cayley isomorphism (ChatGPT / GPT-5.6, Claude, Gemini Deep Think, AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, OpenAI's Astra list of August 2026) and found no AI system credited with anything in the BI-group literature. The OpenAI Astra list I saw only through secondary reports (not the OpenAI page), and none of its items concerns Cayley graphs or BI-groups. Knuth's 'Claude's Cycles' (March 2026) concerns a three-dimensional directed graph's Hamiltonian decomposition; one blog calls the structure a Cayley digraph, but that is not the BI question and I did not open the paper. The only AI-credited Babai-named paper is the 2026 minimal Cayley graph paper, a namesake. Limits: the AI check for most events went only as far as the abstract, which is what I could read; the 2015 and 2019 texts are unread.
competing_reading: The 2015 and 2017 results could be read as making the BI problem partly settled: the 2015 paper, if its examples are as reported, gives known non-BI groups, and the 2017 preprint classifies BI-groups up to order 30 and separates BI from CI for two non-abelian groups. A later pass could then count the problem as partly resolved before the window with no event inside it. Against this: the Wikipedia statement asks for all finite groups and still marks the question open, and nothing inside the window moves it. In the other direction, the windowed CI and DCI results (Ryabov 2025; Dobson, Morris and Spiga 2024) and the minimal Cayley graph results could be argued to move a neighbouring question, but they concern different properties and do not change the BI statement.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full text of Comm. Algebra 43(12), 5159-5167 (2015): its main theorem and whether it exhibits non-BI groups, and which ones. (b) The full text of J. Algebra Appl. 18(1) (2019), article 1950013: the order-30 list, its method (hand or computer), and whether the journal version corrects the v1 'Theorem ??' gaps. (c) A survey or later paper that states the current BI status of specific families (for example, groups of prime-power order or small orders beyond 30); none found in 34 searches. (d) The text of Babai's 1979 Problem 3.3, to confirm whether it asks about digraphs as the search summaries report. (e) A citation search on MathSciNet or zbMATH for the 2015, 2017 and 2019 papers and for the 1979 paper, looking for any paper that discusses BI-groups; neither database was reachable.
